subject: environmental-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the natural capital model, the ongoing yield of goods and services that can be harvested without depleting the resource base is termed:
questions.explain: Natural income is the sustainable yield of resources and services derived from natural capital, analogous to interest on a financial stock.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a transformation rather than a transfer?
options: Leaves falling from a tree to the ground
Photosynthesis converting light energy into chemical energy
Water flowing downstream in a river
questions.explain: A transformation involves a change in the form, state or chemical nature of energy or matter, as when light energy becomes chemical energy in photosynthesis.

questions.q: Someone who believes scientific and technological innovation can overcome environmental problems while allowing continued economic growth holds a primarily:
questions.explain: A technocentric worldview has strong faith in technology and human ingenuity to manage and solve environmental challenges.

questions.q: An isolated system is best defined as one that exchanges:
options: Matter but not energy with its surroundings
Energy but not matter with its surroundings
Neither energy nor matter with its surroundings
Both energy and matter with its surroundings
questions.explain: An isolated system exchanges neither energy nor matter and exists only as a theoretical model, such as the universe as a whole.

questions.q: Which factor generally tends to INCREASE the resilience of an ecosystem?
questions.explain: Higher biodiversity provides functional redundancy and more pathways for recovery, increasing resilience to disturbance.

questions.q: An ecological deficit occurs when a population's:
options: Ecological footprint exceeds the biocapacity available to it
Natural income exceeds its natural capital
questions.explain: An ecological deficit arises when the ecological footprint of a population is greater than the biocapacity of the area it occupies.

questions.q: In the systems approach, which term describes a system that exchanges energy but NOT matter with its surroundings?
questions.explain: A closed system exchanges energy across its boundary but not matter, as approximated by the Earth's global biogeochemical cycles.

questions.q: Systematic monitoring of an environmental variable over many years primarily provides data on:
options: Long-term trends and changes against a baseline
The economic value of a resource only
questions.explain: Long-term monitoring reveals trends and deviations from a baseline, essential for detecting environmental change such as climate or pollution shifts.

questions.q: A renewable natural resource is being used sustainably when:
options: Its rate of use exceeds its rate of replenishment
It is exploited as fast as technologically possible
It is converted entirely into a non-renewable form
Its rate of use equals or is below its rate of natural replenishment
questions.explain: Sustainable use of a renewable resource keeps consumption at or below the natural replenishment rate, preserving the capital stock.

questions.q: A major limitation of environmental models is that they:
options: Are always less useful than a single field measurement
Are simplifications that depend on assumptions and may not capture all real-world complexity
questions.explain: Models are simplified representations whose outputs are only as reliable as their assumptions and the data used to build them.

questions.q: On the spectrum of environmental value systems, which sequence runs from most nature-centred to most technology-centred?
questions.explain: The conventional spectrum runs ecocentric (nature-centred) through anthropocentric to technocentric (technology-centred).

questions.q: The mark-release-recapture (Lincoln index) method is used primarily to estimate the:
questions.explain: Mark-release-recapture estimates the population size of mobile animals by comparing marked and unmarked individuals in a later sample.

questions.q: Negative feedback within a system tends to:
options: Amplify a change and drive the system away from equilibrium
Counteract a change and return the system towards equilibrium
Have no effect on the system's state
questions.explain: Negative feedback counteracts a deviation, restoring the system towards its original equilibrium and promoting stability.

questions.q: Which change would most likely INCREASE a country's per-capita ecological footprint?
options: Increased per-capita consumption of fossil fuels and imported goods
A shift from a meat-rich to a plant-based diet
Higher recycling rates and reduced food waste
questions.explain: Higher per-capita fossil fuel use and resource consumption increase the land and carbon-absorbing area required, raising the footprint.

questions.q: A key strength of using computer models in environmental science is that they:
options: Allow prediction and testing of scenarios that would be impractical or unethical to run in reality
Remove the need for any field data
questions.explain: Models let scientists simulate complex or future scenarios safely, though their reliability depends on the quality of input data and assumptions.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of natural capital?
options: A forest providing timber, oxygen and flood protection
questions.explain: Natural capital refers to natural resources and ecosystems, such as forests, that yield a flow of goods and services (natural income).

questions.q: The precautionary principle suggests that:
options: Only proven impacts should be regulated
Where there is risk of serious harm, lack of full certainty should not prevent preventive action
Economic costs always outweigh environmental risks
Action should be delayed until full scientific certainty of harm is established
questions.explain: The precautionary principle advocates preventive action against plausible serious or irreversible harm even without full scientific certainty.

questions.q: An environmental value system that places humans at the centre, valuing nature for the resources and services it provides to people, is described as:
questions.explain: Anthropocentrism is human-centred, valuing the environment primarily for its utility to humans.

questions.q: The capacity of a system to resist disturbance and recover to its original state is termed its:
questions.explain: Resilience is the ability of a system to absorb and recover from disturbance while retaining its essential function and structure.

questions.q: The ecological footprint is best defined as:
options: The area of land and water required to sustainably provide a population's resources and absorb its wastes
The carbon stored in a forest per hectare
The number of species in a given ecosystem
The total mass of an organism's waste
questions.explain: The ecological footprint estimates the productive land and water area needed to supply a population's resources and assimilate its waste.

questions.q: An ecocentric value system is best characterised by:
options: A nature-centred, holistic view valuing all living things and natural processes
Faith in technology to solve environmental problems
Belief that humans should fully manage and control ecosystems
questions.explain: Ecocentrism is nature-centred and holistic, valuing ecological balance and the intrinsic worth of all living things over human interests.

questions.q: In systems terminology, the amount of a component held within a system, such as carbon in a forest, is called a:
questions.explain: A storage (or stock) is the quantity of energy or matter held within a system at a given time, distinct from the flows that move between storages.

questions.q: Random sampling within a habitat is used mainly to:
options: Deliberately target areas of high biodiversity
Avoid bias and obtain a representative sample of the area
Reduce the total number of samples needed to one
questions.explain: Random sampling minimises observer bias so that the sample is statistically representative of the whole habitat.

questions.q: In ecological field studies, a quadrat is most appropriately used to estimate the:
options: Abundance or percentage cover of plants and sessile organisms
questions.explain: Quadrats sample a defined area to estimate abundance, density or percentage cover of plants and slow-moving or stationary organisms.

questions.q: Which best describes a steady-state equilibrium?
options: A system whose properties fluctuate around a stable average over time
A system that is permanently and irreversibly changing
A system that has reached absolute zero activity
A system with no inputs or outputs
questions.explain: In a steady-state equilibrium, inputs and outputs continue but the system's properties oscillate around a constant long-term average.

questions.q: A line or belt transect is the most suitable sampling method when investigating:
options: Changes in community composition along an environmental gradient
The total population of a single mobile species
A uniform habitat with no environmental variation
questions.explain: Transects sample systematically along a gradient (e.g. shore or altitude) to reveal how communities change with abiotic conditions.

questions.q: The melting of polar ice reducing albedo, causing more solar absorption and further warming and melting, is an example of:
questions.explain: This is positive feedback because the initial change (melting) is amplified, driving the system further from its original state.

questions.q: A transfer in a system is characterised by:
options: Movement of energy or matter without changing its form
A change in the state of energy
The creation of new matter within the system
A change in chemical composition of matter
questions.explain: A transfer moves energy or matter through a system without altering its form, such as water flowing through a pipe or food passing along a food chain.

questions.q: Sustainable development was famously defined by the Brundtland Report as development that:
options: Prioritises conservation over all human activity
Meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Maximises economic output regardless of environmental cost
questions.explain: The 1987 Brundtland definition emphasises meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

questions.q: Intrinsic value, in environmental ethics, refers to the idea that nature:
options: Has value only if it can be technologically managed
Is valuable only for the resources it provides to humans
Should be valued solely in monetary terms
Has worth in its own right, independent of its usefulness to humans
questions.explain: Intrinsic value holds that organisms and ecosystems have worth in themselves, regardless of any utility to humans.
